cues.text: On September 3, 2016,

a research vessel named Martin Bergmann
was heading north through the Canadian
Arctic.

Its crew was going to join the search for
HMS Terror,

one of two ships that had disappeared
during an expedition led by John Franklin.

The main search was taking place much
farther north.

But Sammy Kogvik, a local man aboard the
vessel,

had told another crew member about
something he had seen years earlier:

a large wooden object rising out of the
ice in a bay called Terror Bay.

It was an observation, not proof that a
ship lay below.

The crew changed course anyway and went to
examine the bay.
Erebus had been found two years earlier.
Terror was still missing.
Before Erebus was found,

searchers knew where Franklin's crews had
abandoned the ships,
but not where either had finally sunk.
In May 1845,

Erebus and Terror sailed from England to
search for the Northwest Passage,

a sea route through the Arctic connecting
the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.

There were 129 people aboard the two
ships, under Franklin's overall command.

In September 1846, both vessels became
trapped in ice near King William Island.
Franklin died in June 1847.
By April 1848,
the 105
surviving

members of the expedition had abandoned
the ships and planned
to travel south.

They recorded those events in a note left
in a stone shelter.

The note was written in 1848, but
searchers did not find it until 1859.

It established where the ships had been
trapped
and where the crews had left them.

It did not establish where the hulls
finally came to rest.

A ship abandoned in ice might not remain
at the place where its crew
walked away.

Anyone searching for Erebus and Terror had
to reckon with that difference.
The crews' note was not the only evidence.
Before it was found,
Inuit people

living and travelling in the region had
already shared accounts of encounters
connected to the expedition.

the explorer John Rae received accounts
from Inuit people about Europeans

travelling south and about the bodies of
men found later.

An Inuit interpreter and guide, William
Uligpak, also known as Mar-ko,

played an important part in communicating
this information.

Rae also obtained objects that Inuit
people had collected
after the expedition disappeared.
These reports did not locate a wreck.
They did, however,

describe events beyond the position
recorded in Franklin's note.

Charles Hall later gathered further Inuit
accounts,

working with the interpreters and guides
Takulittuk and Ipiivik.

Some of the accounts described a ship seen
among the ice farther south,

away from the place where the crews had
abandoned their ships.
That ship was said to have sunk.

The descriptions could not, by themselves,
identify it as Erebus or Terror.

But they pointed toward a different part
of the coast.

an Inuit man named Inukpudjijuk indicated
an area
to Hall on a map and made his own sketch.

The area he indicated lay near the
Adelaide Peninsula,

in a southern region known in Inuit
accounts as Ugyulik.

Inukpudjijuk had not witnessed the
sinking,

and his indication was not exact
coordinates.

But it gave the accounts a specific
geographical reference.

The 1848 note showed where the crews had
left the ships.

Inuit accounts suggested a vessel had
later been seen farther south.
Neither identified a wreck,

but the southern coast had become a place
worth searching.
For decades, searches found neither wreck.
In the twentieth century,

David Woodman revisited Inuit testimony
recorded by nineteenth-century
investigators.

He compared descriptions of ships, coastal
landmarks,
and encounters with Franklin's men,

using them to consider possible search
areas.

Woodman joined searches himself but did
not find the ships.

In Gjoa Haven, Inuit historian Louie
Kamookak collected accounts from elders,
studied local place names,
and related historical descriptions

to the geography known by the region's
residents.

Names written down by nineteenth-century
visitors did not always match
modern charts.

Understanding the places named in old
accounts

required knowledge of the actual coast,
islands, and waters.

Kamookak's work was rooted in the region's
own history,

not simply in the search for the British
ships.

Woodman and Kamookak joined a search in
1997 with Parks Canada and other
partners.
No ship was found.

Parks Canada continued working with
Kamookak,

whose research drew on accounts passed
down by elders.
Recorded testimony, local knowledge,

and field searches contributed in
different ways;

none amounted to ready-made wreck
coordinates.

In 2008, underwater archaeologists from
Parks Canada began a multiyear search.
They reviewed historical records and Inuit

accounts and consulted local knowledge
holders.
They identified two principal areas:

one near where the ships had been
abandoned in 1848,

and another farther south, where Inuit
accounts had placed a vessel.

Parks Canada archaeologists scanned the
seabed with sonar,
using sound to image underwater objects.

Government of Nunavut archaeologists
examined sites on land,
including former Inuit camps.

Inuit knowledge holders contributed
history and geography.

Coast guard and other survey teams
supported the work.

Several seasons passed without a confirmed
wreck.
Then, on September 1, 2014,

a Government of Nunavut archaeology team
landed on a small
island in the southern search area.

They were investigating traces of an Inuit
camp,

including a stone outline where a dwelling
had once stood.
During the survey,

a pilot named Andrew Stirling noticed a
rusted piece of metal on the shore.
Archaeologists
examined it and recognized

part of a ship's mechanism for raising and
lowering a boat.

Its design corresponded to equipment shown
in drawings of Erebus.
The team also found a wooden plug used

to close a hole through which a ship's
rope passed.
Neither object pinpointed a wreck,

but both connected that stretch of shore
with shipboard equipment.

Archaeologist Douglas Stenton carried the
finds
to the icebreaker Sir Wilfrid Laurier,

where members of the search team were
based.
The following morning,

Parks Canada archaeologist Ryan Harris
changed the area to be surveyed.

Instead of continuing the sonar work as
previously planned,

the team moved its planned sonar survey
closer

to the shore where the objects had been
found.

The research boat Investigator began
scanning the seabed.

Within minutes, a large ship's hull
appeared on the sonar screen.

After years of searches, a wreck had been
located.
Underwater archaeologists

examined its construction and compared it
with historical plans.

They confirmed that the vessel was HMS
Erebus.
On September 2, 2014,

one of Franklin's two missing ships had
finally been found,

in the southern search area near the
Adelaide Peninsula.

The discovery did not come from exact
coordinates preserved in an old account.

The team had studied a place on land,
recognized potentially relevant objects,
and then shifted the search on the water.

A previously broad search area had
produced a confirmed location.
Terror, however, was still missing.

In 2016, the main search focused farther
north,

closer to where the crews had abandoned
the vessels.

Martin Bergmann was heading there when
Kogvik's report prompted a detour.

Kogvik had seen the object about six years
earlier on a hunting trip.
His observation did not identify a ship.

Other stories in Gjoa Haven had also
described an unknown vessel in Terror Bay.

The Martin Bergmann crew, working with the
Arctic Research Foundation,
chose to investigate.
They surveyed the bay with sonar.

On the seabed was the shape of a large,
three-masted ship,
sitting nearly upright on its keel.

It lay roughly a hundred kilometres from
the main search area.

An underwater vehicle then provided views
of well-preserved parts of the wreck,
including interior spaces.
The images showed that a ship was there.
They did not yet establish its name.

The Arctic Research Foundation informed
Canadian authorities of the discovery.

Parks Canada specialists came to Terror
Bay to examine it archaeologically.
They studied underwater

images and compared visible features with
the historical plans,

including details of the steering
equipment and the bow.

Those features distinguished the wreck
from Erebus.
On September 18, 2016,

Parks Canada formally confirmed that the
ship found in Terror
Bay was HMS Terror.
The discoveries followed different leads.

In 2014, finds on shore changed a sonar
survey and led to Erebus.

Kogvik's report led a vessel to a
different bay and the wreck of Terror.
In each case,

a location was tested and the evidence
underwater was examined
before a ship was identified.

Erebus lay south of King William Island,
near the Adelaide Peninsula.

Terror lay in Terror Bay, beside King
William Island.

What had been uncertain areas on a chart
became two identified wreck sites,
found in 2014 and 2016.

More than a century and a half after the
crews abandoned their ships,
both locations were known.

The search for Franklin's two missing
vessels had reached its end:
Erebus and Terror had been found.
